author: A Robot
objectives: Identify and name the four heart chambers, four heart valves, and major vessels entering and leaving the heart.
Trace the path of blood through pulmonary and systemic circulation in correct sequence.
Distinguish pulmonary circulation from systemic circulation and explain the different roles of the right and left heart.
Explain why the left ventricle has a thicker myocardium than the right ventricle based on pressure and resistance demands.
Describe how atrioventricular and semilunar valves prevent backflow during the cardiac cycle.

modules.description: Students compare an intact exterior heart model with a cutaway heart model to learn anatomical orientation and patient-based right-left terminology.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Orient the heart with apex inferior and slightly toward the patient's left.
Explain why the patient's right and left are reversed from the viewer's perspective in an anterior view.
Recognize major exterior vessel landmarks before studying internal flow.
instructions: View the intact heart on the left and the cutaway heart on the right.
Use the scene controls to rotate the paired models if available.
Remember that anatomical right and left refer to the patient, not the viewer.

components.text: Heart orientation: exterior and cutaway views
Patient's RIGHT appears on viewer's left; patient's LEFT appears on viewer's right.

clips.changeMeaning: The exterior and cutaway heart models are placed side by side so students can compare surface anatomy with internal anatomy.
clips.narration: We begin with two views of the same human heart. The intact model shows the exterior surface and major vessels. The cutaway model removes the anterior wall to reveal chambers, septum, and valves.

clips.changeMeaning: A right-left orientation label appears to clarify anatomical perspective and prevent confusion when viewing the anterior heart.
clips.narration: Anatomical right and left always refer to the patient. In an anterior view, the patient's right side appears on your left, and the patient's left side appears on your right.

components.text: Apex: inferior and toward patient's left. Base: major vessels attach superiorly.

clips.changeMeaning: The apex arrow and vessel glow appear to identify the inferior-left apex and the large vessels at the base of the heart.
clips.narration: The apex points inferiorly and slightly toward the patient's left. At the superior base of the heart, major vessels enter and leave: the venae cavae, pulmonary arteries and veins, and aorta.

modules.description: A guided tour highlights the four chambers, four valves, and major vessels on a cutaway heart while linking them to exterior landmarks.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Identify right atrium, right ventricle, left atrium, and left ventricle.
Identify tricuspid, pulmonary, mitral/bicuspid, and aortic valves and state what each separates.
Identify superior vena cava, inferior vena cava, pulmonary arteries, pulmonary veins, and aorta.
instructions: Watch each highlighted structure and read its label.
Compare the cutaway highlight with the exterior landmark highlight.
Note that mitral valve and bicuspid valve are two names for the same valve.

components.text: Structure label
Structural tour: chambers, valves, vessels

clips.changeMeaning: The tour models appear with no highlight so the learner can prepare for a systematic identification sequence.
clips.narration: This structural tour proceeds in three groups: chambers first, then valves, then major vessels.

components.text:
Chambers:
Right atrium → Right ventricle
Left atrium → Left ventricle

clips.changeMeaning: The chamber highlight shifts through the four chamber locations and the label lists their names in the order emphasized by the tour.
clips.narration: Identify the four chambers: right atrium, right ventricle, left atrium, and left ventricle. The atria are receiving chambers; the ventricles are pumping chambers.

components.text:
Valves:
Tricuspid, Pulmonary,
Mitral/Bicuspid, Aortic

clips.changeMeaning: The highlight narrows to the valve plane to emphasize where blood passes between chambers or from ventricles into outflow vessels.
clips.narration: The four valves maintain one-way flow. The tricuspid valve separates right atrium and right ventricle. The pulmonary valve separates right ventricle and pulmonary trunk. The mitral, or bicuspid, valve separates left atrium and left ventricle. The aortic valve separates left ventricle and aorta.

components.text:
Major vessels:
SVC, IVC, pulmonary arteries,
pulmonary veins, aorta

clips.changeMeaning: The highlight moves to the vessel attachments and the label names each major vessel entering or leaving the heart.
clips.narration: The superior and inferior vena cava return systemic venous blood to the right atrium. Pulmonary arteries carry blood to the lungs. Pulmonary veins return blood to the left atrium. The aorta carries blood to the body.

modules.description: Blue and red animated flow pathways show deoxygenated and oxygenated blood through pulmonary and systemic circuits.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Interpret blue flow as deoxygenated and red flow as oxygenated.
Describe the right heart as the pump to the pulmonary circuit.
Describe the left heart as the pump to the systemic circuit.
instructions: Follow the blue and red pathways through the cutaway heart.
Compare the pulmonary loop near the lungs with the systemic loop representing the body.
Remember that pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood and pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood.

components.text: Blue = deoxygenated; Red = oxygenated

clips.changeMeaning: The cutaway heart and color key establish the visual language for oxygenation status before animated flow begins.
clips.narration: In this scene, blue represents deoxygenated blood, and red represents oxygenated blood.

components.text: Right heart + pulmonary arteries: deoxygenated blood

clips.changeMeaning: The blue flow appears on the right heart and pulmonary arterial pathway to indicate deoxygenated blood moving toward the lungs.
clips.narration: The right side of the heart handles deoxygenated blood. It receives blood from the body and pumps it through the pulmonary arteries toward the lungs.

components.text: Left heart + pulmonary veins + aorta: oxygenated blood

clips.changeMeaning: The red flow appears on the pulmonary venous, left-heart, and aortic pathway to show oxygenated blood moving to the body.
clips.narration: The left side of the heart handles oxygenated blood. It receives blood from pulmonary veins and pumps it through the aorta to the body.

components.text: Pulmonary circuit: heart ⇄ lungs | Systemic circuit: heart ⇄ body

clips.changeMeaning: The lungs and systemic loop models appear to separate the short pulmonary circuit from the longer body-wide systemic circuit.
clips.narration: The pulmonary circuit runs between heart and lungs. The systemic circuit runs between heart and body tissues. Together they form dual circulation.

modules.moduleName: Scene 4: Step-by-Step Red Blood Cell Trace
modules.description: A single enlarged red blood cell is advanced through the complete circulation pathway, changing from blue to red in the lungs and back to blue after systemic exchange.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Trace the full blood flow sequence from vena cava through heart, lungs, heart again, aorta, body, and return.
Identify where blood becomes oxygenated and where it becomes deoxygenated.
Name each chamber, valve, and vessel in order during the route.
instructions: Press Next to move the blood cell to the next structure.
Read the label at each step and rehearse the full path aloud.
Replay until you can trace the route without prompts.

components.text: Start: superior vena cava
Superior vena cava → Right atrium

clips.changeMeaning: The blue blood cell begins in the superior vena cava and moves toward the right atrium to start systemic venous return.
clips.narration: A deoxygenated blood cell returns from the body through the superior vena cava and enters the right atrium.

components.text: Tricuspid valve → Right ventricle

clips.changeMeaning: The cell moves through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle to demonstrate right atrioventricular flow.
clips.narration: The right atrium contracts, pushing the cell through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle.

components.text: Pulmonary valve → Pulmonary trunk → Pulmonary arteries → Lungs

clips.changeMeaning: The cell travels through the pulmonary valve, pulmonary trunk, and pulmonary arteries toward the lung model.
clips.narration: The right ventricle contracts, sending the cell through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary trunk and pulmonary arteries to the lungs.

components.text: Lung capillaries: oxygenation → Pulmonary veins → Left atrium

clips.changeMeaning: The cell changes from blue to red in the lungs and moves through pulmonary veins into the left atrium to show oxygen uptake and return.
clips.narration: In lung capillaries, the cell picks up oxygen and becomes red. It then returns through pulmonary veins to the left atrium.

components.text: Mitral/Bicuspid valve → Left ventricle

clips.changeMeaning: The red cell passes through the mitral or bicuspid valve into the left ventricle, reinforcing left atrioventricular flow.
clips.narration: The left atrium contracts, pushing the oxygenated cell through the mitral, or bicuspid, valve into the left ventricle.

components.text: Aortic valve → Aorta → Systemic circulation → Systemic veins → SVC

clips.changeMeaning: The cell exits to systemic circulation and then returns blue to the superior vena cava, completing the loop.
clips.narration: The left ventricle pumps the cell through the aortic valve into the aorta and systemic circulation. After delivering oxygen, it returns blue through systemic veins to the superior vena cava.

modules.description: Two ventricular cross-sections compare right and left ventricular myocardium thickness and relate wall thickness to pressure demands.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Compare approximate right ventricular wall thickness of 3–5 mm with left ventricular thickness of 10–15 mm.
Explain why the systemic circuit requires higher pressure than the pulmonary circuit.
Relate myocardial wall thickness to the workload of each ventricle.
instructions: Compare the highlighted walls on the two cross-sections.
Use the labels and scale marker to estimate the approximate three-to-one thickness relationship.
Connect the anatomy to the different pressures required by each circuit.

components.text: Right ventricle ~3–5 mm; Left ventricle ~10–15 mm

clips.changeMeaning: Two cross-sections appear at matching anatomical level so students can make a direct left-right ventricular wall comparison.
clips.narration: These cross-sections are cut through the ventricles at the same level so you can compare wall thickness directly.

components.text: Right ventricle myocardium: approximately 3–5 mm

clips.changeMeaning: The right ventricular wall highlight appears with a scale marker to show its relatively thin myocardium.
clips.narration: The right ventricle has a thinner wall, often about three to five millimeters, because it pumps only to the low-pressure pulmonary circuit.

components.text: Left ventricle myocardium: approximately 10–15 mm; about three times thicker

clips.changeMeaning: The left ventricular wall highlight appears larger to show its substantially thicker myocardium and greater pressure-generating role.
clips.narration: The left ventricle has a much thicker wall, about ten to fifteen millimeters, because it pumps blood through the entire body against higher resistance.

components.text: Function: pulmonary circuit = lower pressure; systemic circuit = higher pressure

clips.changeMeaning: Both wall highlights remain visible while the label summarizes the structure-function relationship between thickness and circuit pressure.
clips.narration: The thickness difference is a structure-function relationship: more myocardium allows the left ventricle to generate the higher pressure required for systemic perfusion.

modules.moduleName: Scene 6: Valve Function and Backflow Prevention
modules.description: Open and closed valve models demonstrate atrioventricular and semilunar valve behavior during ventricular filling and contraction.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Classify tricuspid and mitral valves as atrioventricular valves.
Classify pulmonary and aortic valves as semilunar valves.
Explain which valves are open or closed during ventricular filling and ejection.
Describe how valve closure prevents backflow.
instructions: Compare open and closed valve models as they swap states.
Track whether atrioventricular or semilunar valves are open in each phase.
Use the arrows to distinguish forward flow from blocked backflow.

components.text: Valve function: one-way flow
AV valves: tricuspid, mitral | Semilunar valves: pulmonary, aortic

clips.changeMeaning: The valve-focused cutaway appears and the label introduces atrioventricular and semilunar valve categories.
clips.narration: The tricuspid and mitral valves are atrioventricular valves. The pulmonary and aortic valves are semilunar valves. Together, they maintain one-way flow.

components.text: Relaxation/filling: AV open; semilunar closed

clips.changeMeaning: Open AV valves and closed semilunar valves are shown to represent ventricular relaxation and filling.
clips.narration: During ventricular relaxation and filling, atrioventricular valves are open and semilunar valves are closed. Blood moves from atria into ventricles, while arterial backflow is blocked.

components.text: Contraction/ejection: AV closed; semilunar open

clips.changeMeaning: Closed AV valves and open semilunar valves replace the previous state to represent ventricular contraction and outflow.
clips.narration: During ventricular contraction, atrioventricular valves close to prevent backflow into atria, and semilunar valves open so blood can enter the pulmonary trunk and aorta.

components.text: Closed valves prevent backflow and preserve one-way circulation.

clips.changeMeaning: Closed valve models and blocked-flow arrow summarize how valves seal openings and prevent reverse movement.
clips.narration: A closed valve forms a seal. AV valves prevent backflow into atria; semilunar valves prevent backflow into ventricles.

modules.description: An unlabeled cutaway heart highlights structures and presents candidate names for active recognition practice with feedback.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Identify unlabeled chambers, valves, and vessels from location and connections.
Differentiate similar left- and right-sided heart structures.
Use feedback to reinforce correct anatomical terminology.
instructions: Choose the correct name for each highlighted structure.
Use surrounding chambers and vessels as clues.
Repeat the quiz for additional practice.

components.text: Which structure is highlighted?
A. Right atrium  B. Left ventricle  C. Aorta  D. Pulmonary valve
Feedback
Structure Identification Quiz

clips.changeMeaning: The unlabeled heart appears to transition students from guided viewing to active structure identification.
clips.narration: Now identify structures without labels. A highlight will appear, and candidate names will be shown.

components.text: A. Right atrium  B. Left ventricle  C. Aorta  D. Pulmonary valve

clips.changeMeaning: The right atrium is highlighted and options appear to assess recognition of the systemic venous receiving chamber.
clips.narration: Question one. Which chamber receives blood from the superior and inferior vena cava?

components.text: Correct: Right atrium

clips.changeMeaning: Feedback confirms the right atrium and links it to systemic venous return.
clips.narration: Correct answer: right atrium. It receives deoxygenated systemic venous blood from the venae cavae.

components.text: A. Tricuspid  B. Pulmonary  C. Mitral/Bicuspid  D. Aortic

clips.changeMeaning: The highlight moves to the left atrioventricular valve to test recognition of the mitral or bicuspid valve.
clips.narration: Question two. Which valve lies between the left atrium and left ventricle?

components.text: Correct: Mitral/Bicuspid valve

clips.changeMeaning: Feedback confirms the mitral or bicuspid valve and reinforces its two accepted names.
clips.narration: Correct answer: mitral valve, also called the bicuspid valve. It separates the left atrium from the left ventricle.

components.text: A. Superior vena cava  B. Pulmonary artery  C. Pulmonary vein  D. Aorta
Correct: Aorta

clips.changeMeaning: The aorta is highlighted and feedback identifies it as the main systemic outflow vessel from the left ventricle.
clips.narration: This highlighted vessel is the aorta. It receives oxygenated blood from the left ventricle through the aortic valve and distributes it to the body.

modules.moduleName: Scene 8: Blood Flow Tracing Quiz and Recap
modules.description: Students predict the next structure in the blood flow pathway, then review the five major concepts covered in the lab.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Predict the next structure in the circulation sequence from a given location.
Distinguish pulmonary arteries from pulmonary veins by direction and oxygenation status.
Summarize structural inventory, dual circuits, blood pathway, wall thickness asymmetry, and valve function.
instructions: Read each prompt and select the next structure in the flow path.
Pay special attention to pulmonary artery versus pulmonary vein direction.
Review the recap panel before completing the lab.

components.text: Blood is in the right atrium. What comes next?

A. Tricuspid valve
B. Pulmonary veins
C. Aortic valve
D. Left atrium
Feedback
Recap

clips.changeMeaning: The blood flow quiz heart, cell, and prompt appear to begin active sequence prediction.
clips.narration: This quiz asks you to identify the next structure in the path of circulation. Think about one-way flow before answering.

components.text: Blood is in the right atrium. What comes next?

A. Tricuspid valve
B. Pulmonary veins
C. Aortic valve
D. Left atrium
Answer: Tricuspid valve → right ventricle.

clips.changeMeaning: The first quiz prompt tests that blood in the right atrium next passes through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle.
clips.narration: If blood is in the right atrium, the next structure is the tricuspid valve, followed by the right ventricle.

components.text: Blood is leaving the right ventricle for the lungs. Which vessel carries it?

A. Pulmonary arteries
B. Pulmonary veins
C. Aorta
D. Inferior vena cava
Answer: Pulmonary arteries carry blood away from the heart to the lungs.

clips.changeMeaning: The quiz cell moves toward the lungs and the prompt targets the common confusion about pulmonary arteries and veins.
clips.narration: Pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood away from the right ventricle to the lungs. Pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood back to the left atrium.

components.text: Blood is in the left ventricle. What comes next?

A. Tricuspid valve
B. Pulmonary valve
C. Aortic valve
D. Superior vena cava
Answer: Aortic valve → aorta → systemic circulation.

clips.changeMeaning: The quiz cell turns red in the left ventricle and learners identify the aortic valve and aorta as systemic outflow.
clips.narration: From the left ventricle, oxygenated blood exits through the aortic valve into the aorta and systemic circulation.

components.text:
1. Structures: chambers, valves, vessels
2. Dual circuits: pulmonary and systemic
3. Full blood path through the heart
4. Left ventricle wall is thicker than right
5. Valves prevent backflow

clips.changeMeaning: The quiz objects hide and a recap panel appears with the first major concept areas highlighted.
clips.narration: Recap: you identified chambers, valves, and vessels, and distinguished pulmonary circulation from systemic circulation.

components.text: You should now be able to identify structures, trace blood flow in order, compare pulmonary and systemic circuits, explain ventricular wall thickness, and describe valve function.

clips.changeMeaning: The recap highlight shifts to the blood path, ventricular wall thickness, and valve function lines to close the lab with structure-function integration.
clips.narration: You also traced a unit of blood through the full circuit, explained why the left ventricle is thicker, and described how valves prevent backflow.
